title: API Rate Tiering and Contract Versioning Playbook
author: Priya Desai
content:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook codifies how Redwood teams should design, publish, and evolve HTTP/REST and streaming inference APIs with explicit rate tiers, backward-compatibility guards, and operational controls for graceful degradation. It is intended for API owners, SDK maintainers, platform engineers, and on-call SREs.

Scope: Applies to all public and internal inference endpoints (hosted Redwood API, Dedicated public endpoints, and Private control-plane integrations). Does not change existing per-product pricing (finance).

Goals
- Provide a small, auditable set of 'contract tiers' with clear allowed change types per tier.
- Standardize rate limit tiers and request-level backpressure semantics to make consumer expectations predictable.
- Define rollout and deprecation workflows that minimize customer impact and enable automated guardrails.
- Tie observability SLOs and alerting to contract tiers for operational clarity.

Key definitions
- Contract: The API surface (endpoints, request schema, response schema, headers, error types) that clients program against.
- Tier: A classification of a contract (Stable-Public, Stable-Internal, Experimental). Tiers determine allowed changes, SLAs, and testing requirements.
- Minor Compatible Change: Additive schema changes that do not break clients (new optional fields, expanded enums with documented fallbacks).
- Major Breaking Change: Removal or incompatible renaming of fields, semantic changes to existing behavior that require client updates.

Contract tiers and allowed changes
1) Stable-Public
- Intended for external customers, SDKs, and public docs.
- Allowed changes: documentation clarification, additive optional fields, performance improvements that are transparent to clients.
- Not allowed: semantic changes, field removal, reinterpretation of existing fields.
- Versioning: semver-style major.minor.patch where major=breaking. Major increments require deprecation window and migration tooling.
- Rolling policy: Canary -> Gradual rollout (>=24h) -> Global.

2) Stable-Internal
- For internal platform integrations and cross-team contracts with tighter SLAs.
- Allowed changes: additive fields after coordination, minor bugfixes, safe performance optimizations.
- Not allowed without coordination: breaking changes.
- Versioning: minor version pinning supported. Owner must publish migration notes internally.

3) Experimental
- For prototype endpoints, feature flags, and early SDKs. Breaking changes allowed; use short-lived versions and clearly label.
- No SLA guarantees.

Change classification matrix (summary)
- Patch: backwards-compatible bug fix (no schema change). Allowed on all tiers.
- Minor: additive, backwards-compatible change. Allowed on Stable-* and Experimental but requires release notes for Stable-Public.
- Major: breaking change. Allowed for Experimental. For Stable-Public / Stable-Internal: must follow deprecation process (see Rollout & Deprecation).

Rate tiers and throttling policy
- Per-tenant rate tiers (default shown):

| Tier name | Burst RPS | Sustained RPS | Token bucket refill | Target latency (p95) | Intended users |
|-----------|-----------:|--------------:|--------------------:|----------------------:|----------------|
| free | 20 | 5 | 5 tokens/sec | 1500 ms | trial & developer sandbox |
| standard | 200 | 50 | 50 tokens/sec | 600 ms | self-serve production |
| dedicated | 2000 | 800 | 800 tokens/sec | 200 ms | Reserved Dedicated customers |
| internal | 1000 | 500 | 500 tokens/sec | 300 ms | Internal platform apps |

Notes: The above table is the canonical default. Product teams may request tier additions via the API governance board; changes require capacity planning and cost impact analysis.

Request-level backpressure and hedging
- Clients must honor 429 (Too Many Requests) and Retry-After headers. Implement exponential backoff with jitter: base=500ms, factor=2, max=60s.
- Server-side: when queue lengths exceed soft thresholds, return 429 with a Retry-After and a guidance payload (JSON) describing expected retry window and alternative lightweight endpoints (if available).
- Hedging: allowed for idempotent read-only endpoints only. For generation endpoints (non-idempotent), hedging is disabled unless using request_idempotency_id header and server-side deduplication.

Standard headers and metadata
- Required request headers (all tiers):
  - Authorization: Bearer <token>
  - X-Client-Id: <client-id> (used for billing & throttling)
  - X-Client-Version: <semver>
  - X-Request-ID: <uuid> (if not provided server will generate one)
- Optional telemetry headers: X-Routing-Region, X-Preferred-Model, X-Forwarded-For (internal use only)

Compatibility and deprecation workflow
1) Proposal: Owner files Change Request (CR) describing change, rationale, impact, rollout plan, and migration guide. CR must include test plan and perf/regression checks.
2) Impact analysis: Verify backward-compatibility using automated contract tests and real traffic replay (when applicable).
3) Communication: For Stable-Public, publish deprecation notice in docs, SDK repos, and email notification to customers 90 / 60 / 30 days before breaking change.
4) Migration window: For breaking changes, maintain the previous major version for a minimum of 180 days or as negotiated with customers.
5) Forced migration exception: Security fixes may shorten windows — must be approved by Security + CTO.

Rollout checklist (owner must complete before global rollout)
- Register CR in api-governance board and get approval.
- Update API docs and SDK changelogs.
- Create canary deployment (<=1% traffic) for 24–48 hours. Monitor p95 latency, error rate, and cost-per-token.
- After canary: incrementally 10%, 25%, 50%, 100% over 24–72 hours, with automated abort on thresholds.
- Post-rollout: publish post-rollout report with SLI deltas and mitigation steps.

Automated abort thresholds (default)
- p95 latency regression > 30% over baseline for two consecutive monitoring windows (5m) -> abort rollout.
- Error rate (5xx) increase > 2x baseline and >0.5% absolute -> abort.
- Token cost increase > 20% without commensurate latency improvement -> abort and revert.

Operational observability and SLOs
- Each Stable-Public endpoint must publish the following SLOs in dashboards: availability (99.9% monthly for hosted), p95 latency, server error rate (5xx), and throttling rate (429).
- Recommended metrics: request_count, success_count, error_count_by_code, latency_p50/p95/p99, queue_depth, throttled_count, average_tokens_per_request, cost_per_1000_tokens.
- Alerting: set page-channeled alerts for availability degradation and high error rate; slack-only alerts for non-actionable regressions.

Example configuration snippet (service-level)

service_name: text-generation-v2
contract_tier: Stable-Public
default_rate_tier: standard
canary_policy: 1% traffic, 24h
abort_thresholds:
  p95_latency_pct: 30
  error_rate_multiplier: 2
  absolute_error_rate_pct: 0.5
owner: team-text-inference@redwood.ai

Example curl request (including headers and Retry-After handling)

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v2/generate
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
  -H 'X-Client-Id: my-app'
  -H 'X-Client-Version: 1.4.2'
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
  -d '{"prompt":"Summarize our 2025 Q4 roadmap in three bullets","max_tokens":120}'

// Client retry pseudo-code:
// retry_count = 0
// while retry_count < MAX:
//   resp = http.post(...)
//   if resp.status == 429:
//     wait = parse_retry_after(resp.headers) || base * 2**retry_count + jitter
//     sleep(wait)
//     retry_count += 1
//   else:
//     return resp

Ownership, review cadence and enforcement
- API owners must be a named on-call team (owner field) and conduct quarterly compatibility reviews for Stable-Public contracts.
- The API Governance Board (cross-functional: API owners, SDK, SRE, Security, Product) meets weekly to triage CRs and approve major changes.
- Enforcement: CI gate checks (contract tests + schema diffs) will block merges that violate tier rules; the api-governance board can grant exceptions.

Related policies and links
- See: client-backpressure-hedging-and-timeouts (internal) for hedging details.
- Refer to infra-standards capacity planning for major tier additions.

Appendix: FAQ
Q: When do we create a new major version vs. keep compatibility shims?
A: Create a major when a semantic change affects expected client behavior. If server-side shims can preserve semantics with acceptable cost, prefer backwards-compatible approaches and schedule a major for later.

Q: How are rate tiers enforced for Private deployments?
A: Private customers can opt out of Redwood global rate tiers; dedicated or private capacity agreements should specify custom rate tiers in the contract and be enforced by the Private control plane.

Q: Who approves emergency breaking changes?
A: Security critical changes must be approved by Security + CTO with post-facto communication to customers and API Governance Board.
